newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK health reforms weigh on casualty dept.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK health reforms weigh on casualty dept.

text.p: It's Monday afternoon in the casualty ward at St George's hospital and routine work has been suspended while doctors and nurses struggle, in vain, to resuscitate a woman who has suffered a heart attack.
Outside the resuscitation room, psychiatric patient Tommy Sullivan has bitten the end off a glass sample bottle and is wielding its jagged edge at a security guard.
All 17 beds in the department are occupied by patients waiting for treatment or to be moved to wards elsewhere in the south London hospital.
Three patients lie on trolleys in the middle of the room and another three are lined up in wheelchairs waiting for beds.
A 94-year-old woman with a suspected broken pelvis is shrieking abuse at a male nurse as he tries to take her blood pressure. A male voice groans in the next cubicle.
Outside in the waiting room, an electronic sign tells patients they will have to wait five hours before they can hope to be admitted.
This is a typical Monday at St George's.
The casualty departments of London's hospitals hit a crisis this winter, when the cold weather and a flu epidemic stretched their limited resources to breaking point and beyond.
Patients were left lying on hospital trolleys for up to 30 hours while staff tried to find them beds.
GOVERNMENT REFORMS PARTLY TO BLAME
There are many reasons for the increasing burden placed on casualty units, among them the rising elderly population and the perpetual shortage of beds.
The Conservative government's reforms to the health service during 18 years in power are partly to blame.
A huge proportion of the patients who come to Accident and Emergency have ailments like stomach pains and influenza which should have been dealt with by their family doctor.

But changes in the way family doctors -- known as general practitioners -- work mean patients may have to wait several days for an appointment. If they call at night, patients are likely to be offered an agency doctor and it seems people prefer to go to hospital rather than see a stranger.

Psychiatric patients, released from hospital under the government's controversial "Care in the Community" programme, -- in which mentally ill patients are released from hospital and eased back into normal life -- pose another huge problem for Accident and Emergency units.
Such patients make up a large proportion of the homeless sleeping on London's streets. Many are drug addicts or alcholics in addition to their mental problems.

Once released from psychiatric hospitals they have to be readmitted through the casualty units where they can pose a physical threat to staff and other patients as well as taking up valuable time and resources.

In addition to Sullivan, who is being monitored by a television camera in the sealed room where he is now lying curled up on a mattress on the floor, there are three other "care in the community" patients waiting to be seen.
Two such men were brought in by ambulance and a frightened, bewildered-looking woman who refuses to stay in the side room where nurses placed her now hovers in the doorway.

The men, who have the dirt-ingrained skin of people who sleep rough, are sitting in wheelchairs, leaning over a frail elderly man admitted with a bladder problem and cursing one another in slurred voices.
Nurse Mark Ainsworth-Smith pauses from the constant telephone calls and the stream of newly-arrived patients to quieten them.

After a few moments of peace, one of the men lights up a hand-rolled cigarette -- smoking is strictly forbidden. A nurse remonstrates with him and pours water over the cigarette before retreating quickly.
The patient starts unloading his pockets and a large plastic bag onto Ainsworth-Smith's desk, all the time shouting abuse at anyone in the line of his red-eyed, unsteady gaze.
Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell has conceded that mental health services, especially in London, are inadequate, and promised to review them.

But there has been no pledge so far of more funding or new hospitals. A report by a health research body said the government needed to spend at least 59 million pounds ($95 million) to address the shortage of psychiatric beds in London.
HEALTH A KEY ELECTION ISSUE
The health service will be one of the hottest issues in Britain's coming election. Opinion polls show 49 percent of the population place it top of their political priorities.

The opposition Labour Party has pledged to cut bureaucracy by abolishing the "internal market" introduced by the Conservatives under which doctors and even departments within a hospital must buy services from one another.

Hospital departments run to tight budgets and are allowed to carry out only a certain number of operations through the financial year. So if the budget for, say heart by-pass operations, is exhausted patients will have to wait until the following year for treatment.

One consequence of the changes, most of which were introduced in 1989, has been a huge increase in managerial staff, while the number of nurses in the National Health Service (NHS) has been cut by 50,000 in the past five years.
Unlike other departments at St George's, the Accident and Emergency unit will not turn patients away if it exceeds its budget.
"As long as we can show that we had not mismanaged the money, we would be allowed to keep going," said administrator Nigel Morris.
Some accident units, however, did turn patients away last winter and one announced it would not treat patients over the age of 75. Another said it would not treat certain types of patient.

St George's unit suffers from a shortage of money. It has only two consultants, but needs five, says Morris. It also needs While hospital managers favour increasing the number of consultants, the decision is up to the local authority which has been ordered to cut health spending by several million pounds.

The burden on St George's looks certain to grow next year when nearby St Mary's hospital is expected to close. Morris expects an extra 25,000 casualty patients a year as a result, in addition to the 85,000 St George's already sees.
Dozens of hospitals have closed in recent years and their operations moved to single, large sites for greater efficiency. St George's was created by merging three hospitals.
Despite its size, the hospital has to juggle each day to find enough beds for its patients.

Nationwide, the number of NHS hospital beds has been cut by 43,000 since 1990, according to the public service union, UNISON. Some hospitals have had to drive patients hundreds of miles (kilometres) to other hospitals in search of beds.
Recent changes in medical thinking partly justify the cut in the number of hospital beds.
Patients are now advised to get up and move around soon after an operation, rather than lying in bed for days, while advances like keyhole surgery mean recovery times are shorter.
Nevertheless, says Aileen Power, ward manager at St George's, some patients are being sent home too early.
"Its depressing when we see patients come back a few days after we've discharged them," she said.
In the accident unit, a "care in the community" patient has got tired of waiting and is shouting abuse from his wheelchair.
Ainsworth-Smith tries to explain that he can't discharge him until he has seen a doctor, especially as the man says he has taken six sleeping pills and 12 tranqillisers. But he won't be calmed.
The police are called for the third time in a day.
